        "title": "Elicit: AI for scientific research",
        "description": "# AI for Scientiﬁc Research\nElicit helps researchers be 10x more evidence-based\n\nTry now\n\n## Research takes many forms\n### Research reports\n•\n\n[Learn more](https://elicit.com/solutions/reports)\n\n![Elicit interface showing a screening recommendation for a magnesium study with extracted supporting quotes on study design](https://framerusercontent.com/images/HWjzdbSRG0wlQesU2KMjp1h1og.png?width=879&height=542)\n\n### Systematic literature review\n- Elicit can automate screening and data extraction of systematic reviews, while partially supporting search and report generation.\n\n## How we’re different\n### Scale\nElicit can find up to 1,000 relevant papers and analyze up to 20,000 data points at once.\n\n### Accuracy\nElicit is the most accurate AI product for scientific research. Learn about [how we validated Elicit's accuracy.](https://blog.elicit.com/elicit-reports-eval/)\n\n## Latest releases\n- [![Research Agents](https://framerusercontent.com/images/EPxWaAY9GVrY3jf2STaX1flQgA.jpg?width=3980&height=2356)\\\n\\\nJul 17, 2026\\\n\\\nEvaluating Elicit’s Paper Search\\\n\\\nElicit outperformed five other search systems on BioASQ, retrieving more of the papers biomedical experts rely on.](https://elicit.com/blog/evaluating-elicit-paper-search)\n- [![](https://framerusercontent.com/images/cneC5Alt0vudg19YDcxoOU7A52Y.png?width=4284&height=2361)\\\n\\\nMay 6, 2026\\\n\\\nEvaluating Elicit’s Systematic Literature Review Capabilities\\\n\\\nElicit hit 95% search recall, 97% abstract screening, 99% full-text screening, and 96% extraction across 994 Cochrane reviews.](https://elicit.com/blog/evaluating-elicit-slr)\n\n## Trusted by top research institutions\nOur team and our customers have rigorously tested and evaluated Elicit's accuracy\n\nVDI / VDE used Elicit's data extraction for a systematic review informing German education policy. Elicit correctly extracted 1,502 out of 1,511 data points, an accuracy rate of 99.4%.\n\n99.4%\n\nData extraction accuracy\n\n11x\n\nMore evidence considered\n\n[Read VDI/VDE case study](https://blog.elicit.com/case-study-vdi-vde-it/)",

        "title": "Systematic Literature Reviews | Elicit: Al for scientific research",
        "description": "# Systematic Literature Reviews\n## State of the art accuracy\n80%\n\nTime savings\n\n[99.5%](https://elicit.com/blog/evaluating-elicit-slr)\n\nUp to 99.5% screening recall\n\n[96%](https://elicit.com/blog/evaluating-elicit-slr)\n\nData extraction accuracy\n\n[138M](https://support.elicit.com/en/articles/14758040-elicit-s-source-for-papers)\n\nPapers and clinical trials to include in your review\n\n**how it works**\n\n## Elicit helps accelerate every step of a systematic review\n### Screen each paper\nScreen up to 40,000 papers in real-time.\n\nElicit autosuggests screening criteria and recommendations. You can agree, edit, or add your own.\n\nEvery decision is PRISMA-auditable with exclusion reasons, per-criterion scores, and supporting quotes. Dual review pairs two humans with AI assistance, or uses AI as the second reviewer\n\nStep 4\n\n### Extract data\nData extraction is one of Elicit's superpowers. Elicit has the most accurate data extraction of any AI product, including from tables and figures, where most clinical outcomes actually live.\n\nWe can extract both quantitative and qualitative data. Every extraction is supported by quotes or figures from the source.\n\nIterate with our AI-suggested data extraction templates, or create your own.\n\n![Elicit interface extracting quantitative data, such as safety thresholds, from multiple research papers into a summary table](https://framerusercontent.com/images/tle7ZXJTSkUgyf7z0wXfBAzXGU.png?width=590&height=430)\n\nStep 5\n\n## Researchers especially   love these features\n### Dynamic screening & extraction\nElicit's interactive screening & data extraction help you explore the literature in real-time so that you can refine what you're looking for.\n\n![Elicit interface showing a high-relevance study recommendation (4.8/5) with an AI-generated explanation for its inclusion.](https://framerusercontent.com/images/4rFhD8Ei1vsPe6g3fXrauCcyNk.png?width=1965&height=1014)\n\n### Accuracy & precision\n- We've rigorously trained and validated Elicit's accuracy. Elicit can analyze detailed information such as PFS, adverse effects, and detailed interventions or outcomes by trial arm at levels of accuracy exceeding human extraction.\n\n## Validation & impact\nOur team and our customers have rigorously tested and evaluated Elicit's accuracy\n\nVDI / VDE used Elicit's data extraction for a systematic review informing German education policy. Elicit correctly extracted 1,502 out of 1,511 data points, an accuracy rate of 99.4%.\n\n99.4%\n\nData extraction accuracy\n\n11x\n\nResearchers at CSIRO, Australia's national science agency, compared Elicit to manual data extraction and found that Elicit had near-zero false negatives, meaning it did not miss any key information.\n\n363\n\nData points compared to manual extraction\n\n0\n\nFalse negatives; no key information missed\n\nOur team also validates accuracy by comparing Elicit results to the results of published systematic reviews.         "url": "https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/research-synthesis-methods/article/using-elicit-ai-research-assistant-for-data-extraction-in-systematic-reviews-a-feasibility-study-across-environmental-and-life-sciences/C97DAEC70C3173A260F0B12E729E7250",
        "title": "Using Elicit AI research assistant for data extraction in systematic reviews",
        "description": "# Using _Elicit_ AI research assistant for data extraction in systematic reviews: A feasibility study across environmental and life sciences\n## 2 Methods\n### 2.3 Analyses and reporting\nFurther, we also considered results across the type of extracted data (Yes/No, number, categorical, or free text string answers) and by the category of extracted information (study scope/design vs. reporting practice assessment).\n\nWe expressed “Accuracy” of extractions by _Elicit_ as the percentage of the matching pairs of values out of the total pairs of values used in a given comparison ( _Elicit_ vs. gold standard). For the prompt development phase, we expressed “Success” as instances where accuracy exceeded the threshold of 87% (i.e., at least 7 out of 8 values per variable were extracted correctly by _Elicit_). For the testing phase (TEST) and the two re-testing phases (RETEST, HATEST), we reported accuracy as well as reasons for potential mismatches.\n\n### 2.4 Deviations from the protocol\nThird, rather than rating data extracted by _Elicit_ as either match (fully matching human-extracted data), partial (matching some but not all available information extracted by humans), or mismatch (completely different answer from human-extracted data), we simplified the coding to binary values (match = 1) and (mismatch = 0). Depending on the variable, partial matches were still informative (i.e., could be considered as a match), but not for others (mismatch), depending on the context.\n\nFourth, on 16 May 2025, _Elicit_ announced that all columns would now default to “high accuracy” to provide “the most reliable paper extractions across all plans.” Previously, _Basic_/ _Plus Elicit_ plan users had limited access to high-accuracy columns (one per table). A change to a high-accuracy algorithm can be expected to significantly influence the accuracy of data extractions. To test this expectation, on 26 June 2025, we repeated all extractions from the testing phase (HATEST phase; with the high-accuracy algorithm) and compared the results to the earlier extractions from the testing phase (TEST; without the high-accuracy algorithm) and against the human-extracted gold standard answers.\n\nFifth, we had to exclude from our analyses three variables that failed in RETEST and HATEST phases due to human error in prompt specifications (misspecified answer structures). This deviation reduced our total sample sizes to 536 (out of the planned 560) answer values for analyses in these two project stages only.\n\n## 3 Results\n### 3.2 Test phase success and accuracy of Elicit\nDuring the main testing phase (TEST), we used _Elicit_ to extract 70 variables that were deemed successful during the development phase. We used a new sample of eight studies from each of the seven systematic reviews, with 10 variables tested per review (successful variables from the prompt development phase).\n\nOverall, 48 out of the 70 tested variables (69%) reached the expected accuracy threshold of at least 87% at this stage (i.e., at least 7/8 _Elicit_ answers assessed as matching human-extracted gold standard answers). Across the seven reviews, the overall success rates ranged from 50% (Yang et al. [Reference Yang, Liu and Pan30](https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/research-synthesis-methods/article/using-elicit-ai-research-assistant-for-data-extraction-in-systematic-reviews-a-feasibility-study-across-environmental-and-life-sciences/C97DAEC70C3173A260F0B12E729E7250#r30) and Ricolfi et al. [Reference Ricolfi, Vendl and Bräunig24](https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/research-synthesis-methods/article/using-elicit-ai-research-assistant-for-data-extraction-in-systematic-reviews-a-feasibility-study-across-environmental-and-life-sciences/C97DAEC70C3173A260F0B12E729E7250#r24)) to 100% (Lagisz et al. [Reference Lagisz, Zidar and Nakagawa29](https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/research-synthesis-methods/article/using-elicit-ai-research-assistant-for-data-extraction-in-systematic-reviews-a-feasibility-study-across-environmental-and-life-sciences/C97DAEC70C3173A260F0B12E729E7250#r29)), and the extraction accuracy varied across the variables ( [Figure 4](https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/research-synthesis-methods/article/using-elicit-ai-research-assistant-for-data-extraction-in-systematic-reviews-a-feasibility-study-across-environmental-and-life-sciences/C97DAEC70C3173A260F0B12E729E7250#fig4)).\n\nFigure 4\n\nAccuracy of data extractions performed using the _Elicit_ platform when compared to human-extracted gold standard answers. We tested extraction variables that passed the prompt development stage with at least an 87% accuracy (7/8 answers correct) rating ( _y_-axis) for each of the seven systematic reviews ( _x_-axis) using a new test set of eight studies distinct from the prompt development stage per review. The colour of cells in the grid indicates the accuracy (proportion of correct answers) of _Elicit_ data extractions during the testing stage of the project. White cells indicate that a given variable was not tested for a given review.\n\n![](https://static.cambridge.org/binary/version/id/urn:cambridge.org:id:binary:20260529031351247-0197:S1759287926100805:S1759287926100805_fig4.png?pub-status=live)![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)\n\nThe overall extraction accuracy during the prompt development phase and test phase was positively related ( _r_ = 0.38, _t_ = 3.38, df = 68, _p_ = 0.001), indicating that more accurate data extractions during the development phase were also more likely to be accurate during the testing phase. Similarly to the prompt development phase, there was no association between the type of extracted variable and its success (i.e., extraction accuracy above 87%; Chi-squared = 3.88, _df_ = 2, _p_ = 0.275).\n\nWe compared the accuracy of _Elicit_’s data extraction with the accuracy of independent data re-extractions by two human researchers for the 26 variables that were added to the reviews in this project. Using the equivalent subsets of values from the main testing phase, we found that human extractors had fewer mismatches with each other (4/208 = 1.9%) than _Elicit_ had with human gold standard answers (22/208 = 10.6%; Chi-squared = 11.856, _df_ = 1, _p_ = 0.0006). For 13 out of 26 variables, _Elicit_ performed as good as humans (no mismatches), for 12 variables it made more mistakes than humans, and for one it performed better (detecting one mention of sharing study data in Mizuno et al. [Reference Mizuno, Lagisz, Pollo, Yang, Soma and Nakagawa28](https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/research-synthesis-methods/article/using-elicit-ai-research-assistant-for-data-extraction-in-systematic-reviews-a-feasibility-study-across-environmental-and-life-sciences/C97DAEC70C3173A260F0B12E729E7250#r28) review dataset).\n\n### 3.5 Correcting gold standard values based on Elicit data extractions\nHuman-extracted data, even if double-extracted or cross-validated, can contain errors (e.g., due to missing relevant information in the study text or coding errors). After cross-checking mismatches between _Elicit_’s data extractions and our gold standard values, we detected a total of eight human-made errors (<1%; [Supplementary Table S4](http://doi.org/10.1017/rsm.2026.10080)). We corrected these errors and accounted for them when calculating accuracy scores for the data extractions using _Elicit_.\n\n## References\n![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)\n\n[1]\n\nConserv Biol J Soc Conserv Biol. A variable was considered “Successful” if at least seven out of eight answer values were extracted correctly in Elicit, that is, matched human-extracted gold standard values, within a maximum of five iterations of data extraction prompt refinement.         "title": "How we evaluated Elicit Systematic Review",
        "description": "# How we evaluated Elicit Systematic Review\n###### 6 min read\n![How we evaluated Elicit Systematic Review](https://framerusercontent.com/images/MrGTvgTTDMVxabW8QutJw52bG8g.png?width=1500&height=807)\n\nLast month, we introduced [Elicit Systematic Review](https://blog.elicit.com/systematic-review/), a new AI workflow that allows researchers to find papers, screen titles and abstracts, and extract data from full-text papers in 80% less time, without compromising accuracy.\n\nThrough internal and external evaluations, we find that Elicit Systematic Review provides screening and extraction accuracy rivaling humans at a fraction of the cost and labor, ushering in a new era in evidence synthesis.\n\nIn this post, we dive into our evaluation methods and results. In short, we compared Elicit’s screening recommendations to published systematic reviews and found that **Elicit correctly screens in 94% of papers**. We (and independent teams) also compared Elicit's extractions against manual extractions and found that **Elicit extracts data with 94-99% accuracy**.\n\n## 1) Screening performance\n### Methodology\nWe expect researchers using Elicit Systematic Review to start with their own collection of article PDFs identified from other sources (and then augment that collection with Elicit’s search). They can then use Elicit’s Screening step to generate screening recommendations, backed by explanations. This can reduce the amount of time needed to screen thousands of papers from weeks to minutes.\n\n![An image displaying a research tool interface showing automated screening recommendations (Include/Exclude) for academic papers, alongside text describing methodology and performance datasets](https://framerusercontent.com/images/Bg08VJethLsAKmDVw4iWScTrM.png)\n\nWe assessed the quality of Elicit’s screening recommendations by comparing them to the screening decisions made in published systematic reviews.\n\nWe compiled a dataset of 58 published systematic reviews, including articles such as:\n\nWe extracted the main research question from each review to input as a query into Elicit. For example, we extracted “How effective is lithium in treating bipolar depression in adult patients?” from Riedinger et al. 2023.\n\nFor each review, we also asked a large language model to identify which papers the review screened in. Through this, we created a set of “relevant papers” to evaluate Elicit’s recall. Though we verified that all extracted studies were actually screened into their respective review, we did not comprehensively extract all studies from each review. We do not expect this to bias results, given that our screening algorithm uses different technology than the LLM extraction algorithm used here.\n\n![Identification of studies via database and registers: lithiu, in bipolar depression](https://framerusercontent.com/images/sUxdwsGWwQWpgHFA305wh3Lfo4.png)\n\n_Example PRISMA diagram from one of the systematic reviews we used (_ [_Riedinger et al. 2023_](https://www.semanticscholar.org/paper/Lithium-in-bipolar-depression%3A-A-review-of-the-Riedinger-Wee/2ed65ead55e9fc64ee15fa04ca6d19a04d69e0cd?ref=blog.elicit.com) _)._ _The positives in our dataset correspond to the 15 included ones at the bottom._\n\nA good screening engine should also effectively screen out irrelevant papers. To simulate a set of “irrelevant papers” that could be found in a database search, we submitted the 58 queries we extracted in the previous step to Consensus, a popular academic semantic search engine. We added all papers found with this method as irrelevant papers to our dataset, except those that seemed too relevant (since that could bias the results) according to an LLM.\n\n### Results\nGiven this reference set of “relevant papers” and “irrelevant papers”, Elicit:\n\n- **Screened in 93.6% of relevant papers**(recall/sensitivity)\n- **Screened out 62.8% of irrelevant papers**(specificity/true negative rate)\n\nRecall is the most important metric for title and abstract screening, since excluding relevant papers biases results, which is why we built Elicit to excel on this metric.\n\nWe also found that half of the time Elicit improperly screened out papers (thus lowering recall), it was due to improperly generated screening criteria. In practice, systematic reviewers will likely carefully vet Elicit’s screening criteria before screening. Thus, **Elicit’s real-world screening recall, given correctly specified criteria, is ~96.4%**.\n\n![Pie chart showing Elicit's 93.6% recall rate for correctly screening in relevant papers, with a breakdown of errors and a reported 62.8% specificity for filtering irrelevant ones.](https://framerusercontent.com/images/HSuXlmi2SmdVd2udOocsxFttiU.png)\n\nSince Elicit is transparent and editable by design, users can always inspect screening results and override any screening decision.\n\n## 2) Extraction performance\nData extraction is the most laborious and expensive step in systematic reviews, often requiring months of manual effort. Professional researchers are now using Elicit to extract data in 90% less time, enabling them to conduct larger reviews or repurpose their time for deeper per-paper analysis.\n\n![Interface of Elicit's Extraction tool showing a data table of participant characteristics and magnesium interventions, with a side panel displaying supporting quotes and AI-generated explanations.](https://framerusercontent.com/images/XBJvfLqfAYuYu8apYEmrqWwwYw.png)\n\nWe assessed the accuracy of Elicit’s extractions through both internal and external evaluations.\n\n### Internal LLM-based evaluation\nOur internal evaluation consists of using [LLMs to evaluate](https://blog.elicit.com/auto-evaluation/) how well an Elicit extraction compares against manual “gold standard” extractions. While counter-intuitive, we have previously shown that verifying extractions with LLMs has 89% agreement with manual verification.\n\nOur gold standards consist of 128 thoroughly vetted answers to the predefined extraction columns in Elicit, such as “Participant count” or “Study design,” for a given set of papers. The extraction columns generated in Elicit Systematic Review are not identical but generally similar to those predefined questions. Our evaluation method asks an LLM whether the answer generated by Elicit matches the gold standard as well as the text of the paper — we previously found that giving the LLM both a gold standard and the full text provides more trustworthy results than using either in isolation.\n\nAccording to this automated evaluation, Elicit’s data extraction is **94% accurate**.\n\n### VDI/VDE\nThe German consulting firm VDI/VDE advises governments and the private sector on innovation and technology. They recently used Elicit to scale up a systematic review on educational interventions from 50 to 550 papers. They checked Elicit’s results vs. expert manual extraction and found Elicit was 99.4% accurate.\n\n![External evaluation results showing 99.4% accuracy for Elicit in a study by VDI/VDE. The graphic displays 1,502 correct extractions versus 9 incorrect extractions, noting that the tool allows researchers to evaluate 11x more papers.](https://framerusercontent.com/images/cmOTbHzJM7QZ2rQ1HIvRsqTEQNw.png)\n\nThey estimated that Elicit allows them to evaluate 11x more papers per project. Read more in our [VDI/VDE case study](https://blog.elicit.com/case-study-vdi-vde-it/).\n\n## Conclusion\nThrough internal and external evaluations, we find that Elicit is the most rigorous AI systematic review tool available, providing screening and extraction accuracy rivaling humans at a fraction of the cost and labor.\n\nTo further assess Elicit’s Systematic Review, we have separately asked professional researcher evaluators to replicate existing, published reviews using Elicit. We’re excited to share results soon.",

        "url": "https://intuitionlabs.ai/articles/elicit-data-extraction-clinical-papers",
        "title": "Elicit AI Data Extraction Guide for Clinical Papers - IntuitionLabs",
        "description": "## Executive Summary\n**Elicit** is a novel AI-based research assistant that uses LLMs to streamline systematic review tasks, including _semantic paper search_, _screening_, _data extraction_, and _report summarization_ ( [[4]](https://bmcmedresmethodol.biomedcentral.com/articles/10.1186/s12874-025-02528-y#:~:text=Among%20AI%20tools%2C%20Elicit%2C%20based,for%20the%20determination%20of%20specific)) ( [[5]](https://support.elicit.com/en/articles/7927169#:~:text=Elicit%20Systematic%20Review%20guides%20you,through%20each%20of%20these%20steps)).\n\nFollowing the methodology, we present **empirical evidence and case studies** on Elicit’s performance. For example, Elicit’s internal case study in education research reported 99.4% data extraction accuracy ( [[8]](https://elicit.com/solutions/literature-review#:~:text=VDI%20%2F%20VDE%20used%20Elicit%27s,4)), and a CSIRO evaluation found near-zero missed data points. Independent studies using Elicit’s outputs are emerging: for instance, a Cochrane collaboration (Bianchi _et al._, 2025) systematically compared Elicit’s extraction on 20 randomized trials to human extraction, finding that Elicit often captured “more” or “equal” information but sometimes missed detail ( [[9]](https://www.ovid.com/journals/cesm/fulltext/10.1002/cesm.70033/~data-extractions-using-a-large-language-model-elicit-and#:~:text=Data%20extractions%20were%20%E2%80%9Cmore%E2%80%9D%20by,Supporting%20Information%20S1%3A%20Appendix%201)). We contrast these results with other AI methods: for example, a recent proof-of-concept found another LLM (Claude 2) achieved 96.3% accuracy on 160 clinical trial data points ( [[10]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38432227/#:~:text=used%20the%20browser%20version%20of,substantially%20enhance%20the%20efficiency%20and)). We tabulate these findings to highlight accuracy comparisons.\n\nElicit (and LLM tools in general) can greatly speed reviews (through automation of repetitive work) and potentially improve comprehensiveness, but they also require careful [human oversight](https://intuitionlabs.ai/articles/fda-ai-510k-submission-guidelines-best-practices) ( [[9]](https://www.ovid.com/journals/cesm/fulltext/10.1002/cesm.70033/~data-extractions-using-a-large-language-model-elicit-and#:~:text=Data%20extractions%20were%20%E2%80%9Cmore%E2%80%9D%20by,Supporting%20Information%20S1%3A%20Appendix%201)) ( [[11]](https://bmcmedresmethodol.biomedcentral.com/articles/10.1186/s12874-025-02528-y#:~:text=complexity%20of%20the%20research%20,the%20tool%20performance%20are%20increased)). In conclusion, Elicit offers a powerful, 10x-speedup approach to structured data extraction in systematic reviews ( [[13]](https://support.elicit.com/en/articles/7927169#:~:text=With%20AI%20and%20language%20models%2C,the%20end%20of%20the%20process)) ( [[14]](https://bmcmedresmethodol.biomedcentral.com/articles/10.1186/s12874-025-02528-y#:~:text=the%20entire%20systematic%20review%20process,the%20tool%20performance%20are%20increased)). Researchers should leverage Elicit’s capabilities (guided by robust validation and transparency) to enhance efficiency and accuracy in synthesizing clinical evidence, while remaining mindful of its current limitations.\n\n02\n\n## Using Elicit for Structured Data Extraction\n### Overview of the Systematic Review Workflow\n3. **Screening:** In Stage 2, you specify inclusion/exclusion criteria. Elicit auto-generates a draft set of screening criteria based on your question ( [[22]](https://support.elicit.com/en/articles/7927169#:~:text=1,papers%20for%20your%20systematic%20review)) (e.g. “population is adults with diabetes”, “intervention includes drug therapy”). You can edit or add criteria as needed. Elicit then applies these criteria to your gathered papers in two phases: title/abstract screening, followed optionally by full-text screening ( [[34]](https://support.elicit.com/en/articles/7927169#:~:text=Screening)) ( [[11]](https://bmcmedresmethodol.biomedcentral.com/articles/10.1186/s12874-025-02528-y#:~:text=complexity%20of%20the%20research%20,the%20tool%20performance%20are%20increased)). During screening, each paper is scored on how well it matches the criteria, allowing you to quickly accept or reject, with the option to _override_ the AI’s decision ( [[34]](https://support.elicit.com/en/articles/7927169#:~:text=Screening)). Strict criteria (that force exclusion if not met) and adjustable thresholds allow control of sensitivity vs specificity. At the end of screening you have your **narrowed set of included studies** for extraction.\n4. **Define Extraction Fields (Columns):** Prior to auto-extraction, you need to set up the data table columns. Elicit will automatically suggest some relevant columns based on your question and the pilot papers, but you can customize these. For example, for a clinical drug trial SR, columns might include “Population size (N)”, “Intervention dosage”, “Control condition”, “Primary outcome value”, “Confidence Interval”, etc. You can _add new columns, edit instructions, or duplicate existing ones_ ( [[35]](https://support.elicit.com/en/articles/4267649#:~:text=Elicit%20will%20automatically%20add%20suggested,based%20on%20your%20research%20question)). Elicit supports saving column presets for reuse. It is common to refine the column instructions by iterating on a small “pilot set” of ~10 papers. Elicit randomly selects 10 included papers to test-pilot the extraction; you review their extracted values (and supporting quotes) to gauge accuracy ( [[7]](https://support.elicit.com/en/articles/4267649#:~:text=From%20your%20set%20of%20screened,set%20for%20faster%20column%20iteration)). You might adjust the column prompt wording or format at this stage to improve consistency.\n5. **Run Data Extraction:** Once injection of columns and prompts is finalized, you execute **full extraction** on the entire set of included papers ( [[36]](https://support.elicit.com/en/articles/4267649#:~:text=Step%205%3A%20Run%20the%20full,extraction)). Elicit applies each extraction column query across all PDFs. Importantly, it always shows you the supporting quote (text snippet from the paper) that led to each extracted cell ( [[25]](https://support.elicit.com/en/articles/4267649#:~:text=Save%20any%20columns%20you%27d%20like,Save%20as%20preset)) ( [[26]](https://support.elicit.com/en/articles/7927169#:~:text=confirmation%20button%20confirming%20that%20you%27d,from%20your%20paper%20extraction%20allowance)). This allows rapid verification: you can eyeball the highlighted passages if something looks wrong. The extraction may take time for large sets, but Elicit will continue processing in the background. When finished, the result is a structured table (viewable in-app or exportable as CSV) containing the extracted data and references.\n6. **Review & Refine:** After extraction, you should manually review the table. Elicit marks each cell with reasoning text, so you can verify correctness. It’s prudent to correct any errors by clicking into cells and editing the entries (or editing the source quote if misinterpreted). This hybrid AI-human approach ensures accuracy. You may also adjust columns or rerun extraction if needed.\n\n## Data Analysis and Performance Evidence\n### Elicit’s Reported Accuracy\nOfficial data (Elicit’s own case studies) suggest very high accuracy. For instance, VDI/VDE (a German engineering organization) conducted a large systematic review using Elicit. They reported that **1502 of 1511** required data points were correctly extracted automatically – an accuracy of **99.4%** ( [[8]](https://elicit.com/solutions/literature-review#:~:text=VDI%20%2F%20VDE%20used%20Elicit%27s,4)). Similarly, researchers at CSIRO (Australia) benchmarked Elicit against manual extraction and found **near-zero false negatives**, meaning Elicit missed essentially no key information compared to human reviewers ( [[43]](https://elicit.com/solutions/literature-review#:~:text=Researchers%20at%20CSIRO%2C%20Australia%27s%20national,not%20miss%20any%20key%20information)). Elicit’s team also mentions **94–99%** accuracy rates in replicated reviews tested internally ( [[44]](https://elicit.com/solutions/literature-review#:~:text=94%E2%80%9396)). (These figures likely reflect aggregate performance on fields like numerical outcomes.)\n\nThese case-study numbers are **promising**, though they come from internal testing contexts and must be interpreted cautiously. Still, they indicate that _for well-defined fields_, Elicit can reach near-human reliability.\n\n## Case Studies and Perspectives\n- **German Education Policy (VDI/VDE):** In the development of education guidelines, researchers used Elicit to automate a systematic review. They reported _1502/1511_ data points correctly extracted (99.4% accuracy) ( [[8]](https://elicit.com/solutions/literature-review#:~:text=VDI%20%2F%20VDE%20used%20Elicit%27s,4)). This remarkable result, albeit from an internal case, indicates that for well-formatted data (likely numeric and textual items in reports), Elicit can be extremely reliable.\n- **CSIRO (Australia):** A published mention (CSIRO) found that Elicit had near-zero false negatives when compared to manual extraction ( [[43]](https://elicit.com/solutions/literature-review#:~:text=Researchers%20at%20CSIRO%2C%20Australia%27s%20national,not%20miss%20any%20key%20information)). In other words, anything a human found, Elicit also found (or more). The implication is that Elicit is _sensitive_ and casts a wide net. However, it may include irrelevant bits (false positives), which is where human curation is needed.\n- **Bernard _et al._ (France, 2025) – Screening Example:** The BMC study by Bernard _et al._ evaluated Elicit in an umbrella review of smart living environments for aging. They used Elicit to replicate their prior review search. Results: Elicit found 3 additional studies not caught previously ( [[40]](https://bmcmedresmethodol.biomedcentral.com/articles/10.1186/s12874-025-02528-y#:~:text=The%20repeatability%20test%20found%20246%2C169,independent%20umbrella%20review%20search)), but only 17.6% of the original included studies were identified . This highlights that Elicit’s semantic search can compensate for human oversight to some extent (finding new relevant records) but also misses many if used alone. As a result, they conclude Elicit is a helpful _supplement_, not a replacement.\n- **Bianchi _et al._ (Switzerland, 2025) – Extraction Study:** As noted above, this systematic comparison of Elicit vs human on 20 RCTs found that Elicit often captured the same or more detail as the human reviewer ( [[9]](https://www.ovid.com/journals/cesm/fulltext/10.1002/cesm.70033/~data-extractions-using-a-large-language-model-elicit-and#:~:text=Data%20extractions%20were%20%E2%80%9Cmore%E2%80%9D%20by,Supporting%20Information%20S1%3A%20Appendix%201)). It also demonstrated that Elicit’s performance may be higher in some fields (e.g. identifying basic study parameters) than others (complex multi-arm interventions). The authors suggest that Elicit can boost completeness and speed during extraction, but final analysis still requires human judgment on data validity ( [[9]](https://www.ovid.com/journals/cesm/fulltext/10.1002/cesm.70033/~data-extractions-using-a-large-language-model-elicit-and#:~:text=Data%20extractions%20were%20%E2%80%9Cmore%E2%80%9D%20by,Supporting%20Information%20S1%3A%20Appendix%201)) ( [[11]](https://bmcmedresmethodol.biomedcentral.com/articles/10.1186/s12874-025-02528-y#:~:text=complexity%20of%20the%20research%20,the%20tool%20performance%20are%20increased)).\n- **Panayi _et al._ (2023) – ML Extraction in Oncology:** Though not about Elicit specifically, this study shows the viability of transformer-based extraction in clinical reviews. Their BERT+CRF model for oncology trials achieved solid F1 scores (~70–88%) ( [[17]](https://systematicreviewsjournal.biomedcentral.com/articles/10.1186/s13643-023-02351-w#:~:text=For%20entity%20recognition%2C%20the%20pretrained,pair%20of%20related%20entity%20types)). They emphasize that pretraining on biomedical text improved accuracy significantly. This context implies that Elicit – which presumably is powered by models continuously updated on academic text – likely benefits similarly from domain-specific knowledge.\n- **Polak & Morgan (2024) – Materials Science LLM Extraction:** While in a different field, their ChatGPT-4 “ChatExtract” workflow (zero-shot with prompt engineering) attained ~90% precision/recall ( [[31]](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41467-024-45914-8#:~:text=overcome%20known%20issues%20with%20LLMs,4.%20We)). The methods (iterative question-answering, redundancy) could be conceptually applied to clinical data extraction in Elicit’s design. The high performance reinforces that, with thoughtful prompting, ChatGPT-level models can extract numeric data nearly as well as LLMs specifically trained for data tasks.\n\n## Discussion of Implications and Future Directions\n- **Multipronged AI Strategies:** As seen in Poser’s “LLM consensus” approach ( [[49]](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12946029/#:~:text=Results)), combining outputs from multiple models can increase reliability. Elicit might in future take such an ensemble approach: e.g., running each query through GPT-based and Claude-based backends and reconciling differences. This could potentially lower the error rates further (currently ~4% major errors ( [[9]](https://www.ovid.com/journals/cesm/fulltext/10.1002/cesm.70033/~data-extractions-using-a-large-language-model-elicit-and#:~:text=Data%20extractions%20were%20%E2%80%9Cmore%E2%80%9D%20by,Supporting%20Information%20S1%3A%20Appendix%201)), but consensus might reduce that to negligible levels).\n- **Better Evaluation Metrics:** The community will need standardized benchmarks to assess these tools. Just as there are GLUE benchmarks for NLP, we might see shared extraction tasks for systematic review data (perhaps as extensions of the CADIMA or Cochrane AI projects). Metrics beyond plain accuracy (like completeness, precision-recall on key fields) should be reported. The work by Panayi _et al._ ( [[17]](https://systematicreviewsjournal.biomedcentral.com/articles/10.1186/s13643-023-02351-w#:~:text=For%20entity%20recognition%2C%20the%20pretrained,pair%20of%20related%20entity%20types)) scoring F1 may serve as a template: future studies should use comparable metrics so that performance can be meaningfully aggregated across studies.\n\n## Conclusion\nThis report has examined the methodology and evidence for using **Elicit** to extract structured data from clinical research papers. We have shown that Elicit supports a full systematic review pipeline, from question formulation through to final report, with special emphasis on automating data extraction into tables.\n\nDrawing on case studies and research, we highlighted that Elicit can achieve high accuracy in data extraction – often comparable to trained humans (for example, >95% of data fields correct in internal tests ( [[8]](https://elicit.com/solutions/literature-review#:~:text=VDI%20%2F%20VDE%20used%20Elicit%27s,4)) and independent comparisons showing the same or more information extracted in ~50% of cases ( [[9]](https://www.ovid.com/journals/cesm/fulltext/10.1002/cesm.70033/~data-extractions-using-a-large-language-model-elicit-and#:~:text=Data%20extractions%20were%20%E2%80%9Cmore%E2%80%9D%20by,Supporting%20Information%20S1%3A%20Appendix%201))). Other LLM-based studies (e.g. Claude 2 and GPT-4) similarly demonstrate 90–96% accuracy on clinical data tasks ( [[10]](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38432227/#:~:text=used%20the%20browser%20version%20of,substantially%20enhance%20the%20efficiency%20and)) ( [[31]](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41467-024-45914-8#:~:text=overcome%20known%20issues%20with%20LLMs,4.%20We)). These results indicate that large language models, when guided properly, can substantially reduce the workload of systematic reviews.\n\nWe have emphasized that **human oversight remains essential**. Researchers must carefully check Elicit’s outputs against source texts ( [[25]](https://support.elicit.com/en/articles/4267649#:~:text=Save%20any%20columns%20you%27d%20like,Save%20as%20preset)). We also noted limitations (variable reproducibility ( [[40]](https://bmcmedresmethodol.biomedcentral.com/articles/10.1186/s12874-025-02528-y#:~:text=The%20repeatability%20test%20found%20246%2C169,independent%20umbrella%20review%20search)), occasional errors) and the need for adherence to emerging best-practice guidelines ( [[53]](https://bmcmedresmethodol.biomedcentral.com/articles/10.1186/s12874-025-02528-y#:~:text=Given%20the%20multiplicity%20of%20available,AI%20reporting%20guidelines%20which%20are)). Despite these caveats, Elicit’s potential is clear.\n\nIn conclusion, to effectively use Elicit for structured data extraction:",

        "title": "Evaluating the AI Tool “Elicit” as a Semi-Automated Second Reviewer ...",
        "description": "## Abstract\nSystematic reviews are essential for evidence synthesis but often require extensive time and resources, especially during data extraction. This proof-of-concept study evaluates the performance of _Elicit_, an AI tool specifically developed to support systematic reviews, in the context of a systematic review on psychological factors in dermatological conditions. We compared _Elicit’s_ automated data extraction with manually extracted data across 43 studies and 602 data points. Both were assessed against a consensus-based ground truth. Elicit achieved an overall accuracy of 81.4%, compared to 86.7% for human reviewers—a difference that was not statistically significant. In cases where _Elicit_ and the human reviewer extracted the same information, this information was correct in 100% of instances, suggesting that agreement between human and machine may serve as a reliable proxy for validity. Based on these results, we propose a semi-automated workflow in which _Elicit_ functions as a second reviewer, reducing workload while maintaining high data quality. Our results demonstrate that domain-specific AI tools can effectively augment data extraction in systematic reviews, especially in settings with limited time or personnel.\n\n## Introduction\nWithin systematic reviews, study selection and data extraction are particularly resource-intensive steps ( [Nussbaumer-Streit et al., 2021](https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/10.1177/08944393251404052#bibr53-08944393251404052)).\n\nIn contrast, significantly less evidence exists regarding the use of LLMs for full-text data extraction ( [Hu & Geng, 2024](https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/10.1177/08944393251404052#bibr35-08944393251404052)), despite this step being both time-consuming ( [Gue et al., 2024](https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/10.1177/08944393251404052#bibr27-08944393251404052); [Polanin et al., 2019](https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/10.1177/08944393251404052#bibr56-08944393251404052)) and prone to cognitive strain and errors ( [Garousi & Felderer, 2017](https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/10.1177/08944393251404052#bibr20-08944393251404052); [Mathes et al., 2017](https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/10.1177/08944393251404052#bibr48-08944393251404052)). Reported error rates in human data extraction range from approximately 15% ( [Buscemi et al., 2006](https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/10.1177/08944393251404052#bibr13-08944393251404052)) to 30% ( [Horton et al., 2010](https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/10.1177/08944393251404052#bibr34-08944393251404052); [Zhu et al., 2023](https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/10.1177/08944393251404052#bibr81-08944393251404052)) and up to 45% ( [Tang et al., 2023](https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/10.1177/08944393251404052#bibr71-08944393251404052)). These findings highlight the need for alternative procedures in data extraction, a task that LLMs should theoretically be capable of performing with high accuracy ( [Schmidt et al., 2025](https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/10.1177/08944393251404052#bibr63-08944393251404052)).\n\nAs [Sun et al. (2024](https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/10.1177/08944393251404052#bibr66-08944393251404052), p. 2) summarize their results: “Whilst promising, the percentage of correct responses is still unsatisfactory and therefore substantial improvements are needed for current AI tools to be adopted in research practice.”\n\nFor instance, LLMs extracted incorrect numbers of participants, hallucinated a control group when none was present in the study, or fabricated a numeric answer when the actual answer was missing ( [Gartlehner et al., 2024](https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/10.1177/08944393251404052#bibr21-08944393251404052); [Kartchner et al., 2023](https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/10.1177/08944393251404052#bibr40-08944393251404052); [Schmidt et al., 2025](https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/10.1177/08944393251404052#bibr63-08944393251404052); [Yun et al., 2024](https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/10.1177/08944393251404052#bibr80-08944393251404052)). Even small inaccuracies can have far-reaching consequences, potentially undermining the credibility of the review process and distorting its conclusions ( [Susnjak et al., 2024](https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/10.1177/08944393251404052#bibr68-08944393251404052)).\n\nTo address this challenge, the current study therefore focuses on the proprietary AI-Tool _Elicit_, specifically designed to facilitate the (systematic) literature review process.\n\nTherefore, we were able to not only test the tool’s overall accuracy, that is, its ability to autonomously extract information, but also test whether it could serve as an independent checker for the inevitable human errors, that is, as an alternative to a second human reviewer.\n\n## Method\n### Automated Extraction Using _Elicit_\nTo evaluate the performance of the AI tool _Elicit_, we first randomly selected 3 of the 46 studies and uploaded their full-text PDF files via _Elicit_’s “upload and extract” feature. This function allows users to privately upload their own papers (which remain inaccessible to others) and specify which information should be extracted Using _Elicit_’s “high accuracy mode” (available during Autumn 2024). At that time, the “high accuracy mode” was an optional feature designed to enhance extraction precision by allocating additional computational resources. During this initial trial, we observed that _Elicit_’s “Main Results” column contained less information than its manually extracted counterpart.\n\nFollowing successful calibration on the three pilot studies, the remaining 43 studies were uploaded to a new instance of _Elicit_ using identical prompts.\n\n### Comparison and Validation Procedure\nSubsequently, all 602 data points (43 studies x 7 columns x 2 extraction tables) were independently validated by three authors of the systematic review, using the 43 full papers (46 full papers used in the systematic review minus the 3 papers used in the calibration phase).\n\n_Elicit_’s extractions were exported and compared to the manually created Reviewer 1 tables in a structured, paper-by-paper format (see [Supplemental Material](https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/10.1177/08944393251404052#supplementary-materials), Table Sheet _Elicit_Table_). As the three evaluators were also co-authors of the original systematic review and had contributed to the initial data extraction, a blinding procedure was not applied, as it was neither feasible nor methodologically meaningful in this context. The three authors independently determined whether the corresponding data points in the two extraction tables (one manually created by human “reviewer 1” and one automatically created by “reviewer 2” _Elicit_) provided the same information. Then, the data points were either labeled “correct” or “incorrect.” These consensus decisions based on three independent reviewers are considered the “gold standard” or “ground truth” the human “reviewer 1” and the artificial “reviewer 2” is compared against.\n\nFor instance, for the “Measures” column, for one study, the human rater extracted “DLQI,” whereas _Elicit_ extracted “Dermatology Life Quality Index (DLQI),” which was rated as conveying equivalent information. In the same column, for another study, the human rater extracted “Original,” whereas _Elicit_ extracted “Original questionnaire with 9 half-open tasks, scale from 1 to 10 for categorizing diseases by level of shame, and percentage rating of shame for own disease compared to the most embarrassing disease,” which was rated as diverging in informational content. However, in both examples, both the human as well as the automated extraction were labeled as “correct.” For a third study, the human rater extracted “QASD,” whereas _Elicit_ extracted “Questionnaire for the Assessment of Self-Disgust (QASD), Perceived Stigmatization Questionnaire (PSQ), Brief Symptom Inventory (BSI),” which was again rated as diverging in informational content. In this example, Elicit’s extraction was labeled as “correct,” whereas the human rater’s extraction was labeled as “incorrect,” since it was incomplete and did not provide all relevant measures used in this study.\n\n## Results\n### Extraction of the Same Information\n| Category | Same information extracted | Accuracy | McNemar test | Description of Elicit’s extraction errors |\n|-|-|-|-|-|\n| Human “reviewer 1” | _Elicit_ as “reviewer 2” |\n| --- | --- |\n| Study Design | 0.70 | 0.907 (39/43) | 0.930 (40/43) | Chi2 (1, _N_ = 43) = 0, _p_ = 1 | • In one case, Elicit did not extract the information with sufficient specificity ( [Muftin et al., 2022](https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/10.1177/08944393251404052#bibr51-08944393251404052)). |\n| • In two cases, it mislabeled the underlying study design (e.g., [Buckwalter, 1982](https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/10.1177/08944393251404052#bibr12-08944393251404052)). |\n| Population | 0.74 | 0.907 (39/43) | 0.953 (41/43) | Chi2 (1, _N_ = 43) = 0.17, _p_ = .68 | • In both instances, Elicit extracted data from cited studies rather than from the actual study (a [systematic] review, e.g., [Russo et al., 2004](https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/10.1177/08944393251404052#bibr58-08944393251404052)). |\n| Country/Region | 0.72 | 0.953 (41/43) | 0.953 (41/43) | Chi2 (1, _N_ = 43) = 0, _p_ = 1 | • In one case, the relevant information was in the supplemental material, to which Elicit did not have access ( [van Beugen et al., 2016](https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/10.1177/08944393251404052#bibr75-08944393251404052)). It therefore marked the information as “not available.” The three reviewers nevertheless categorized this as “incorrect,” since a human rater could have simply referred to the supplemental material. |\n| • In one case, the information was not explicitly stated in the article, but from the way the methods section was written, it was clear that it was in the country the authors worked in. The human rater could infer this information, Elicit could not ( [Schienle & Wabnegger, 2022](https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/10.1177/08944393251404052#bibr62-08944393251404052)). |\n| • In cases of [systematic] reviews, Elicit often stated “not mentioned” or “international” or similar, whereas the human rater often extracted the country the first author of the study worked in. The three reviewers categorized this as “not the same information” but both “correct”. |\n| Participant Count | 0.81 | 0.907 (39/43) | 0.884 (38/43) | Chi2 (1, _N_ = 43) = 0, _p_ = 1 | • In one case, Elicit did not differentiate between participants taking part in the qualitative study and participants taking part in the quantitative study but added these participants up to a single participant count ( [Tan et al., 2022b](https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/10.1177/08944393251404052#bibr70-08944393251404052)). |\n| • In three cases, Elicit extracted data from cited studies, not from the actual study (which is a [systematic)] review, e.g., [Russo et al., 2004](https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/10.1177/08944393251404052#bibr58-08944393251404052)). |\n| Constructs of Interest | 0.16 | 0.558 (24/43) | 0.512 (22/43) | Chi2 (1, _N_ = 43) = 0.04, _p_ = .84 | • In most cases, Elicit identified constructs of interest too broadly. For example, it included constructs that were mentioned but not measured, or only referenced indirectly, i.e., that are “related” to the constructs of interest (e.g., [Buckwalter, 1982](https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/10.1177/08944393251404052#bibr12-08944393251404052); [Ginsburg & Link, 1993](https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/10.1177/08944393251404052#bibr26-08944393251404052); [Mento et al., 2020](https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/10.1177/08944393251404052#bibr49-08944393251404052); [Sampogna et al., 2012](https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/10.1177/08944393251404052#bibr59-08944393251404052)). |\n| Measures | 0.12 | 0.930 (40/43) | 0.698 (30/43) | Chi2 (1, _N_ = 43) = 5.78, _p_ = .02 | • In one case, Elicit correctly described a questionnaire used, but this questionnaire was not used to measure one of the constructs of interest ( [O’Neil et al., 2011](https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/10.1177/08944393251404052#bibr55-08944393251404052)). |\n| • In 10 cases, Elicit extracted data from cited studies, not from the actual study (which is a [systematic] review, e.g., [Russo et al., 2004](https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/10.1177/08944393251404052#bibr58-08944393251404052)). |\n| • In one case, Elicit extracted the statistical methods used, not the measurement instruments ( [Schielein et al., 2020](https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/10.1177/08944393251404052#bibr61-08944393251404052)). |\n| • In one case, Elicit extracted the quantitative questionnaires correctly but neglected the qualitative instrument ( [George et al., 2021](https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/10.1177/08944393251404052#bibr24-08944393251404052)). |\n| Main Results | 0.35 | 0.907 (39/43) | 0.767 (33/43) | Chi2 (1, _N_ = 43) = 3.13, _p_ = .08 | • In one review article, Elicit singled out a result from a cited study and presented it as one of the main results ( [Torales et al., 2020](https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/10.1177/08944393251404052#bibr74-08944393251404052)). |\n| • In six cases, Elicit reported results not found in the original article. Analogous to the information extracted in the “Constructs of Interest” column, it was too liberal in relabeling results of constructs that were only “implied” (e.g., [Jafferany & Pastolero, 2018](https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/10.1177/08944393251404052#bibr38-08944393251404052); [Vlăduţ & Kállay, 2010](https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/10.1177/08944393251404052#bibr77-08944393251404052)). |\n| • In one case, Elicit did not strictly distinguish between the study’s own results and results discussed in the cited literature ( [Almeida et al., 2020](https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/10.1177/08944393251404052#bibr1-08944393251404052)). |\n| • In two cases, Elicit’s extraction of the main results was incomplete, possibly due to these results being mainly presented in a table or figure (e.g., [Tan et al., 2022](https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/10.1177/08944393251404052#bibr69-08944393251404052)). |\n| Average | 0.52 | 0.867 | 0.814 |\n\n## Conclusion\n_Elicit_ demonstrates promising accuracy and consistency as a tool for semi-automated data extraction in systematic reviews.
